Whereas other children have <hi type="italic">foolishness bound in their hearts,</hi> which appears in what they say or do, he was <hi type="italic">filled with wisdom,</hi> not by any advantages of instruction and education, but by the operation of the Holy Ghost; every thing he said and did was wisely said, and wisely done, above his years. (3.) Whereas other children show that the corruption of nature is in them, and <hi type="italic">the tares of sin</hi> grow up with the <hi type="italic">wheat of reason,</hi> he made it appear that nothing but <hi type="italic">the grace of God was upon him</hi> (the wheat sprang up without tares), and that, whereas other children are by nature children of wrath, he was <hi type="italic">greatly beloved,</hi> and high in the favour of God; that God loved him, and cherished him, and took a particular care of him.
entries.9ee4847bc6f1a6f6cb25248b4e66e59a8633175e: <div eID="gen25283" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Sitting with the Doctors.</title> <div sID="gen25284" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover. <hi type="super">42</hi> And when he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem after the custom of the feast. 43 And when they had fulfilled the days, as they returned, the child Jesus tarried behind in Jerusalem; and Joseph and his mother knew not <hi type="italic">of it.</hi> <hi type="super">44</hi> But they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among <hi type="italic">their</hi> kinsfolk and acquaintance. <hi type="super">45</hi> And when they found him not, they turned back again to Jerusalem, seeking him. <hi type="super">46</hi> And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions. <hi type="super">47</hi> And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers. <hi type="super">48</hi> And when they saw him, they were amazed: and his mother said unto him, Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing. <hi type="super">49</hi> And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business? <hi type="super">50</hi> And they understood not the saying which he spake unto them. <hi type="super">51</hi> And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them: but his mother kept all these sayings in her heart. <hi type="super">52</hi> And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man. <div eID="gen25284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25285" type="x-p"/> We have here the only passage of story recorded concerning our blessed Saviour, from his infancy to the day of his showing to Israel at twenty-nine years old, and therefore we are concerned to make much of this, for it is in vain to wish we had more. Here is, <div eID="gen25285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25286" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's <hi type="italic">going up with his parents</hi> to Jerusalem, at the feast of the passover, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.41-Luke.2.42">v. 41, 42</reference>. 1. It was their constant practice to attend there, according to the law, though it was a long journey, and they were poor, and perhaps not well able, without straitening themselves, to bear the expenses of it. Note, Public ordinances must be frequented, and we must <hi type="italic">not forsake the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is.</hi> Worldly business must give way to spiritual concerns. Joseph and Mary had a son in the house with them, that was able to teach them better than all the rabbin at Jerusalem; yet they <hi type="italic">went up</hi> thither, <hi type="italic">after the custom of the feast. The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob,</hi> and so should we. We have reason to suppose that Joseph went up likewise at the feasts of <hi type="italic">pentecost</hi> and <hi type="italic">tabernacles;</hi> for all the males were to appear there <hi type="italic">thrice a year,</hi> but Mary only at the <hi type="italic">passover,</hi> which was the greatest of the three feasts, and had most gospel in it. 2. The child Jesus, at <hi type="italic">twelve years old,</hi> went up with them. The Jewish doctors say that at twelve years old children must begin to fast from time to time, that they may learn to fast on the day of atonement; and that at thirteen years old a child begins to be <hi type="italic">a son of the commandment,</hi> that is, obliged to the duties of adult church-membership, having been from his infancy, by virtue of his circumcision, <hi type="italic">a son of the covenant.</hi> It is not said that this was the <hi type="italic">first time</hi> that Jesus went up to Jerusalem to worship at the feast: probably he had done it for some years before, having spirit and wisdom above his years; and all should attend on public worship that can <hi type="italic">hear with understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.8.2">Neh. viii. 2</reference>. Those children that are forward in other things should be put forward in religion. It is for the honour of Christ that children should attend on public worship, and he is pleased with their hosannas; and those children that were in their infancy dedicated to God should be called upon, when they are grown up, to come to the <hi type="italic">gospel passover,</hi> to the Lord's supper, that they make it their own act and deed to join themselves to the Lord. <div eID="gen25286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25287" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's <hi type="italic">tarrying behind his parents at Jerusalem,</hi> unknown to them, in which he designed to give an early specimen of what he was reserved for. <div eID="gen25287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25288" type="x-p"/> 1. His parents did not return till they had <hi type="italic">fulfilled the days;</hi> they had staid there all the seven days at the feast, though it was not absolutely necessary that they should stay longer than the two first days, after which many went home. Note, It is good to stay to the conclusion of an ordinance, as becomes those who say, <hi type="italic">It is good to be here,</hi> and not to hasten away, as if we were like Doeg, <hi type="italic">detained before the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen25288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25289" type="x-p"/> 2. The child <hi type="italic">tarried behind in Jerusalem,</hi> not because he was loth to go home, or shy of his parents' company, but because he had business to do there, and would let his parents know that he had a <hi type="italic">Father in heaven,</hi> whom he was to be <hi type="italic">observant</hi> of more than of <hi type="italic">them;</hi> and respect to <hi type="italic">him</hi> must not be construed disrespect <hi type="italic">to them.</hi> Some conjecture that he tarried behind in the temple, for it was the custom of the pious Jews, on the morning that they were to go home, to go first to the temple, to worship God; there he <hi type="italic">staid behind,</hi> and found entertainment there till they found him again. Or, perhaps, he staid at the house where they lodged, or some other friend's house (and such a child as he was could not but be the darling of all that knew him, and every one would court his company), and went up to the temple only at church-time; but so it was that he staid behind. It is good to see young people willing to <hi type="italic">dwell in the house of the Lord;</hi> they are then like Christ. <div eID="gen25289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25290" type="x-p"/> 3. His parents went the <hi type="italic">first day's journey</hi> without any suspicion that he was left behind, for they <hi type="italic">supposed him to have been in the company,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.44">v. 44</reference>. On these occasions, the crowd was very great, especially the first day's journey, and the roads full of people; and they concluded that he came along with some of their neighbours, and they <hi type="italic">sought him among their kindred and acquaintance,</hi> that were upon the road, going down. Pray did <hi type="italic">you</hi> see our Son? or, Did <hi type="italic">you</hi> see him? Like the spouses's inquiry, <hi type="italic">Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?</hi> This was a jewel worth seeking after. They knew that every one would be desirous of his company, and that he would be willing to do good among <hi type="italic">his kinsfolk and acquaintance,</hi> but among them they <hi type="italic">found him not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.45">v. 45</reference>. There are many, too many, who are our kinsfolk and acquaintance, that we cannot avoid conversing with, among whom we find little or nothing of Christ. When they could not hear of him in this and the other company upon the road, yet they hoped they should meet with him at the place where they lodged that night; but <hi type="italic">there</hi> they could learn no tidings of him. Compare this with <reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.9">Job xxiii. 8, 9</reference>. <div eID="gen25290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25291" type="x-p"/> 4. When they found him not at their quarters at night, they <hi type="italic">turned back again,</hi> next morning, <hi type="italic">to Jerusalem, seeking him.</hi> Note, Those that would find Christ must <hi type="italic">seek till they find;</hi> for he will at length be found of those that seek him, and will be found their bountiful rewarder. Those that have lost their comforts in Christ, and the evidences of their interest in him, must bethink themselves where, and when, and how, they lost them, and must <hi type="italic">turn back again</hi> to the place where they last had them; must <hi type="italic">remember whence they are fallen, and repent, and do their first works,</hi> and <hi type="italic">return to their first love,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.4-Rev.2.5">Rev. ii. 4, 5</reference>. Those that would recover their lost acquaintance with Christ must go to Jerusalem, the <hi type="italic">city of our solemnities,</hi> the place which he has <hi type="italic">chosen to put his name there;</hi> must attend upon him in his ordinances, in the gospel-passover, there they may hope to meet him. <div eID="gen25291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25292" type="x-p"/> 5. The <hi type="italic">third day</hi> they found him <hi type="italic">in the temple,</hi> in some of the apartments belonging to the temple, where the doctors of the law kept, not their courts, but their conferences rather, or their schools for disputation; and there they found him <hi type="italic">sitting in the midst of them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.46">v. 46</reference>), not standing as a <hi type="italic">catechumen</hi> to be examined or instructed by them, for he had discovered such measures of knowledge and wisdom that they admitted him to sit among them as a fellow or member of their society. This is an instance, not only that he was <hi type="italic">filled with wisdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.40">v. 40</reference>), but that he had both a desire to increase it and a readiness to communicate it; and herein he is an example to children and young people, who should learn of Christ to delight in the company of those they may get good by, and choose to <hi type="italic">sit in the midst of</hi> the doctors rather than in the midst of the players. Let them begin at <hi type="italic">twelve years old,</hi> and sooner, to enquire after knowledge, and to associate with those that are able to instruct them; it is a hopeful and promising presage in youth to be desirous of instruction. Many a youth at Christ's age now would have been playing with the <hi type="italic">children in the temple,</hi> but he was sitting with the <hi type="italic">doctors in the temple.</hi> (1.) He <hi type="italic">heard</hi> them. Those that would <hi type="italic">learn</hi> must be <hi type="italic">swift to hear.</hi> (2.) He <hi type="italic">asked them questions;</hi> whether, as a teacher (he had authority so to ask) or as a learner (he had humility so to ask) I know not, or whether as an associate, or joint-searcher after truth, which must be found out by mutual amicable disquisitions. (3.) He returned <hi type="italic">answers</hi> to them, which were very surprising and satisfactory, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.47">v. 47</reference>. And his wisdom and <hi type="italic">understanding</hi> appeared as much in the questions he asked as in the answers he gave, so that all who heard him <hi type="italic">were astonished:</hi> they never heard one so young, no indeed any of their greatest doctors, talk sense at the rate that he did; like David, he had <hi type="italic">more understanding than all his teachers,</hi> yea, <hi type="italic">than the ancients,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.99-Ps.119.100">Ps. cxix. 99, 100</reference>. Now Christ showed forth some rays of his glory, which were presently drawn in again. He <hi type="italic">gave them a taste</hi> (says Calvin) of his divine wisdom and knowledge. Methinks this public appearance of Christ in the temple, as a teacher, was like Moses's early attempt to deliver Israel, which Stephen put this construction upon, that <hi type="italic">he supposed his brethren would have understood,</hi> by that, <hi type="italic">how God by his hand would deliver them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.7.24-Acts.7.25">Acts vii. 24, 25</reference>. They might have taken the hint, and been delivered then, but <hi type="italic">they understood not;</hi> so they here might have had Christ (for aught I know) to enter upon his work now, but they were only <hi type="italic">astonished,</hi> and <hi type="italic">understood not</hi> the indication; and therefore, like Moses, he retires into obscurity again, and they hear no more of him for many years after. <div eID="gen25292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25293" type="x-p"/> 6. His mother talked with him privately about it. When the company broke up, she took him aside, and examined him about it with a deal of tenderness and affection, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.48">v. 48</reference>. Joseph and Mary were both <hi type="italic">amazed</hi> to find him there, and to find that he had so much respect showed him as to be admitted to <hi type="italic">sit among the doctors,</hi> and to be taken notice of. His father knew he had only the name of a father, and therefore said nothing. But, (1.) His mother told him how ill they took it: "<hi type="italic">Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us?</hi> Why didst thou put us into such a fright?" They were ready to say, as Jacob of Joseph, "<hi type="italic">A wild beast has devoured him;</hi> or, He is fallen into the hands of some more cruel enemy, who has at length found out that he was the young child whose life Herod had sought some years ago." A thousand imaginations, we may suppose, they had concerning him, each more frightful than another. "Now, why hast thou given us occasion for these fears? <hi type="italic">Thy father and I have sought thee, sorrowing;</hi> not only troubled that we lost thee, but vexed at ourselves that we did not take more care of thee, to bring thee along with us." Note, Those may have leave to complain of their losses that think they have lost Christ. But their <hi type="italic">weeping</hi> did not hinder <hi type="italic">sowing;</hi> they did not sorrow and sit down in despair, but sorrowed and <hi type="italic">sought.</hi> Note, If we would find Christ, we must seek him <hi type="italic">sorrowing,</hi> sorrowing that we have lost him, that we have provoked him to withdraw, and that we have sought him no sooner. They that thus seek him in sorrow shall find him, at length, with so much the greater joy. (2.) He gently reproved their inordinate solicitude about him (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.49">v. 49</reference>): "<hi type="italic">How is it that you sought me?</hi> You might have depended upon it, I would have followed you home when I had done the business I had to do here. I could not be lost in Jerusalem. Wist ye not that I <hi type="italic">ought to be,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en tois tou patros mou</hi></hi>;—<hi type="italic">in my Father's house?"</hi> so some read it; "where else should the Son be, who <hi type="italic">abideth in the house for ever?</hi> I ought to be," [1.] "<hi type="italic">Under my Father's care</hi> and protection; and therefore you should have cast the care of me upon him, and not have burdened yourselves with it." Christ is a shaft hid in his Father's quiver, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa. xlix. 2</reference>. He takes care of his church likewise, and therefore let us never despair of its safety. [2.] "<hi type="italic">At my Father's work</hi>" (so we take it): "I must be <hi type="italic">about my Father's business,</hi> and therefore could not go home as soon as you might. <hi type="italic">Wist ye not?</hi> Have you not already perceived that concerning me, that I have devoted myself to the service of religion, and therefore must employ myself in the affairs of it?" Herein he hath left us an example; for it becomes the children of God, in conformity to Christ, to attend their heavenly Father's business, and to make all other business give way to it. This word of Christ we now think we understand very well, for he hath explained it in what he hath done and said. It was his errand into the world, and his meat and drink in the world, to do his Father's will, and finish his work: and yet at that time his parents <hi type="italic">understood not this saying,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.50">v. 50</reference>. They did not understand what business he had to do then in the temple for his Father. They believed him to be the Messiah, that should have the throne of his father David; but they thought that should rather bring him to the royal palace than to the temple. They <hi type="italic">understood not</hi> his prophetical office; and he was to do much of his work in that. <div eID="gen25293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25294" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Here is their return to Nazareth. This glimpse of his glory was to be short. It was now over, and he did not urge his parents either to come and settle at Jerusalem or to settle him there (though that was the place of improvement and preferment, and where he might have the best opportunities of showing his wisdom), but very willingly retired into his obscurity at Nazareth, where for many years he was, as it were, buried alive. Doubtless, he came up to Jerusalem, to worship at the feast, three times a year, but whether he ever went again into the temple, to dispute with the doctors there, we are not told; it is not improbable but he might. But here we are told, <div eID="gen25294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25295" type="x-p"/> 1. That he was <hi type="italic">subject to his parents.</hi> Though once, to show that he was <hi type="italic">more than a man,</hi> he withdrew himself from his parents, to attend his heavenly Father's business, yet he did not, as yet, make that his constant practice, nor for many years after, but was <hi type="italic">subject to them,</hi> observed their order, and went and came as they directed, and, as it should seem, worked with his father at the trade of a carpenter. Herein he hath given an example to children to be dutiful and obedient to their parents in the Lord. Being <hi type="italic">made of a woman,</hi> he was made under the law of the fifth commandment, to teach the <hi type="italic">seed</hi> of the faithful thus to approve themselves to him a faithful seed. Though his parents were poor and mean, though his father was only his <hi type="italic">supposed</hi> father, yet he was <hi type="italic">subject to them;</hi> though he was <hi type="italic">strong in spirit,</hi> and <hi type="italic">filled with wisdom</hi> nay though he was the Son of God, yet he was subject to his parents; how then will <hi type="italic">they</hi> answer it who, though foolish and weak, yet are disobedient to their parents? <div eID="gen25295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25296" type="x-p"/> 2. That his mother, though she did not perfectly understand her son's sayings, yet <hi type="italic">kept them in her heart,</hi> expecting that hereafter they would be explained to her, and she should fully understand them, and know how to make use of them. However we may neglect men's sayings because they are obscure (<hi type="italic">Si non vis intelligi debes negligi—If it be not intelligible, it is not valuable</hi>), yet we must not think so of God's sayings. That which at first is dark, so that we know not what to make of it, may afterwards become plain and easy; we should therefore <hi type="italic">lay it up</hi> for hereafter. See <reference osisRef="John.2.22">John ii. 22</reference>. We may find use for that another time which now we see not how to make useful to us. A <hi type="italic">scholar</hi> keeps those grammar rules in memory which at present he understands not the use of, because he is told that they will hereafter be of use to him; so we must do by Christ's sayings. <div eID="gen25296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25297" type="x-p"/> 3. That he improved, and came on, to admiration (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">v. 52</reference>): <hi type="italic">He increased in wisdom and stature.</hi> In the perfections of his divine nature there could be no increase; but this is meant of his human nature, his body increased in <hi type="italic">stature</hi> and bulk, he grew in the growing age; and his soul increased <hi type="italic">in wisdom,</hi> and in all the endowments of a human soul. Though the Eternal Word was united to the human soul from his conception, yet the divinity that dwelt in him manifested itself to his humanity by degrees, <hi type="italic">ad modum recipientis—in proportion to his capacity;</hi> as the faculties of his human soul grew more and more capable, the gifts it received from the divine nature were more and more communicated. And he increased in <hi type="italic">favour with God and man,</hi> that is, in all those graces that rendered him acceptable to God and man. Herein Christ accommodated himself to his estate of humiliation, that, as he condescended to be an infant, a child, a youth, so the image of God shone brighter in him, when he grew up to be a youth, than it did, or could, while he was an <hi type="italic">infant</hi> and a <hi type="italic">child.</hi> Note, Young people, as they grow in stature, should grow in wisdom, and then, as they grow in wisdom, they will grow in favour <hi type="italic">with God and man.</hi>  <chapter eID="Luke.2"/> <div eID="gen25297" type="x-p"/>

entries.f946e4046c3df93ef5a342f9196621ec3f226588: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14265"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.2.1-Luke.2.7">Lu 2:1-7</reference>. Birth of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14265"/><hi type="bold">1. Cæsar Augustus--</hi>the first of the Roman emperors.<div eID="gen27631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the world--</hi>so the vast Roman Empire was termed.<div eID="gen27632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taxed--</hi>enrolled, or register themselves. <div eID="gen27633" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd46102fa75cd672170d0d1e03e38ad87ca29a07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14266"/><div sID="gen27634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14266"/><hi type="bold">2. first ... when Cyrenius, &c.--</hi>a very perplexing verse, inasmuch as Cyrenius, or Quirinus, appears not to have been governor of Syria for about ten years after the birth of Christ, and the "taxing" under his administration was what led to the insurrection mentioned in <reference osisRef="Acts.5.37">Ac 5:37</reference>. That there was a taxing, however, of the whole Roman Empire under Augustus, is now admitted by all; and candid critics, even of skeptical tendency, are ready to allow that there is not likely to be any real inaccuracy in the statement of our Evangelist. Many superior scholars would render the words thus, "This registration was previous to Cyrenius being governor of Syria"--as the word "first" is rendered in <reference osisRef="John.1.15">Joh 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.18">15:18</reference>. In this case, of course, the difficulty vanishes. But it is perhaps better to suppose, with others, that the registration may have been ordered with a view to the taxation, about the time of our Lord's birth, though the taxing itself--an obnoxious measure in Palestine--was not carried out till the time of Quirinus. <div eID="gen27634" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9a976472e1c05ae6cad42e00974cb20e2b9e12d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14267"/><div sID="gen27635" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14267"/><hi type="bold">3. went ... to his own city--</hi>the city of his extraction, according to the Jewish custom, not of his abode, which was the usual Roman method. <div eID="gen27635" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebcd89aae5644bd93d5a085cfcc63df987ece852: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14268"/><div sID="gen27636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14268"/><hi type="bold">4-5. Not only does Joseph, who was of the royal line, go to Bethlehem (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.1">1Sa 16:1</reference>), but Mary too--</hi>not from choice surely in her condition, but, probably, for personal enrollment, as herself an heiress. <div eID="gen27636" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a3a359a0801419071a1e6f664eed3afe6d8012a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14270"/><div sID="gen27638" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14270"/><hi type="bold">6. while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered--</hi>Mary had up to this time been living at the wrong place for Messiah's birth. A little longer stay at Nazareth, and the prophecy would have failed. But lo! with no intention certainly on her part, much less of Cæsar Augustus, to fulfil the prophecy, she is brought from Nazareth to Bethlehem, and at that nick of time her period arrives, and her Babe is born (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.23">Psa 118:23</reference>). "Every creature walks blindfold; only He that dwells in light knows whether they go" [Bishop Hall]. <div eID="gen27638" type="x-p"/>
entries.df7c88eeb0f4d893f2cfcbfb720b1f511a31b716: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14271"/><div sID="gen27639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14271"/><hi type="bold">7. first-born--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Matt.1.25">Mt 1:25</reference>; yet the law, in speaking of the first-born, regardeth not whether any were born after or no, but only that none were born before [Lightfoot].<div eID="gen27639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrapt him ... laid him--</hi>The mother herself did so. Had she then none to help her? It would seem so (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2Co 8:9</reference>).<div eID="gen27640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a manger--</hi>the manger, the bench to which the horses' heads were tied, on which their food could rest [Webster and Wilkinson].<div eID="gen27641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no room in the inn--</hi>a square erection, open inside, where travellers put up, and whose rear parts were used as stables. The ancient tradition, that our Lord was born in a grotto or cave, is quite consistent with this, the country being rocky. In Mary's condition the journey would be a slow one, and ere they arrived, the inn would be fully occupied--affecting anticipation of the reception He was throughout to meet with (<reference osisRef="John.1.11">Joh 1:11</reference>).<div eID="gen27642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Wrapt in His swaddling--</hi>bands,<div eID="gen27643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27644" type="x-p"/> And in His manger laid,<div eID="gen27644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27645" type="x-p"/> The hope and glory of all lands<div eID="gen27645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27646" type="x-p"/> Is come to the world's aid.<div eID="gen27646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27647" type="x-p"/> No peaceful home upon His cradle smiled,<div eID="gen27647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27648" type="x-p"/> Guests rudely went and came where slept the royal Child.<div eID="gen27648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27649" type="x-p"/> Keble<div eID="gen27649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27650" type="x-p"/> But some "guests went and came" not "rudely," but reverently. God sent visitors of His own to pay court to the new-born King. <div eID="gen27650" type="x-p"/>
entries.b90a1249c80b75f7efb62c6ae128cab9e10e93dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14272"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.2.8-Luke.2.20">Lu 2:8-20</reference>. Angelic Annunciation to the Shepherds--Their Visit to the Newborn Babe.</title> <div sID="gen27651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14272"/><hi type="bold">8. abiding in the fields--</hi>staying there, probably in huts or tents.<div eID="gen27651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch ... by night--</hi>or, night watches, taking their turn of watching. From about passover time in April until autumn, the flocks pastured constantly in the open fields, the shepherds lodging there all that time. (From this it seems plain that the period of the year usually assigned to our Lord's birth is too late). Were these shepherds chosen to have the first sight of the blessed Babe without any respect of their own state of mind? That, at least, is not God's way. "No doubt, like Simeon (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.25">Lu 2:25</reference>), they were among the waiters for the Consolation of Israel" [Olshausen]; and, if the simplicity of their rustic minds, their quiet occupation, the stillness of the midnight hours, and the amplitude of the deep blue vault above them for the heavenly music which was to fill their ear, pointed them out as fit recipients for the first tidings of an Infant Saviour, the congenial meditations and conversations by which, we may suppose, they would beguile the tedious hours would perfect their preparation for the unexpected visit. Thus was Nathanael engaged, all alone but not unseen, under the fig tree, in unconscious preparation for his first interview with Jesus. (See on <reference osisRef="John.1.48">Joh 1:48</reference>). So was the rapt seer on his lonely rock "in the spirit on the Lord's Day," little thinking that this was his preparation for hearing behind him the trumpet voice of the Son of man (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Re 1:10</reference>, &c.). But if the shepherds in His immediate neighborhood had the first, the sages from afar had the next sight of the new-born King. Even so still, simplicity first, science next, finds its way to Christ, whom<div eID="gen27652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27653" type="x-p"/> In quiet ever and in shade<div eID="gen27653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27654" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Shepherds and Sage may find--</hi> <div eID="gen27654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27655" type="x-p"/> They, who have bowed untaught to Nature's sway,<div eID="gen27655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27656" type="x-p"/> And they, who follow Truth along her star-pav'd way.<div eID="gen27656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27657" type="x-p"/> Keble <div eID="gen27657" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c4c450050ad90d5f20329c541a213ac4838a1bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14273"/><div sID="gen27658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14273"/><hi type="bold">9. glory of the Lord--</hi>"the brightness or glory which is represented as encompassing all heavenly visions" [Olshausen].<div eID="gen27658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sore afraid--</hi>So it ever was (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.7">Da 10:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.12">Lu 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.17">Re 1:17</reference>). Men have never felt easy with the invisible world laid suddenly open to their gaze. It was never meant to be permanent; a momentary purpose was all it was intended to serve. <div eID="gen27659" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6039c9b46a7e899111ee0b2eeec2e4ab9e423a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14274"/><div sID="gen27660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14274"/><hi type="bold">10. to all people--</hi>"to the whole people," that is, of Israel; to be by them afterwards opened up to the whole world. (See on <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Lu 2:14</reference>). <div eID="gen27660" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf1917cd24963bdab8f30196393c45337052d0b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14275"/><div sID="gen27661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14275"/><hi type="bold">11. unto you is born--</hi>you shepherds, Israel, mankind [Bengel]. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>, "Unto us a Child is born." It is a birth--"The Word is made flesh" (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>). When? "This day." Where? "In the city of David"--in the right line and at the right "spot"; where prophecy bade us look for Him, and faith accordingly expected Him. How dear to us should be these historic moorings of our faith! With the loss of them, all substantial Christianity is lost. By means of them how many have been kept from making shipwreck, and attained to a certain external admiration of Him, ere yet they have fully "beheld His glory."<div eID="gen27661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a Saviour--</hi>not One who shall be a Saviour, but "born a Saviour."<div eID="gen27662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ the Lord--</hi>"magnificent appellation!" [Bengel]. "This is the only place where these words come together; and I see no way of understanding this "Lord" but as corresponding to the Hebrew Jehovah" [Alford]. <div eID="gen27663" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e005908a558e96b09b12fe2ee92a0729de3dbe7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14276"/><div sID="gen27664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14276"/><hi type="bold">12. a sign--</hi>"the sign."<div eID="gen27664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the babe--</hi>"a Babe."<div eID="gen27665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a manger--</hi>"the manger." The sign was to consist, it seems, solely in the overpowering contrast between the things just said of Him and the lowly condition in which they would find Him--Him whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting, "ye shall find a Babe"; whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, "wrapt in swaddling bands"; the "Saviour, Christ the Lord," lying in a manger! Thus early were these amazing contrasts, which are His chosen style, held forth. (See <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2Co 8:9</reference>.) <div eID="gen27666" type="x-p"/>
entries.c30d8db0359b6e03751f85bc95b31abaf81a93aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14277"/><div sID="gen27667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14277"/><hi type="bold">13. suddenly--</hi>as if only waiting till their fellow had done.<div eID="gen27667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the angel--</hi>who retires not, but is joined by others, come to seal and to celebrate the tidings he has brought.<div eID="gen27668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavenly host--</hi>or "army," an army celebrating peace! [Bengel] "transferring the occupation of their exalted station to this poor earth, which so seldom resounds with the pure praise of God" [Olshausen]; to let it be known how this event is regarded in heaven and should be regarded on earth. <div eID="gen27669" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e9c2e272a35e4d77a034f03fa6843e68adb0f4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14278"/><div sID="gen27670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14278"/><hi type="bold">14. Glory, &c.--</hi>brief but transporting hymn--not only in articulate human speech, for our benefit, but in tunable measure, in the form of a Hebrew parallelism of two complete clauses, and a third one only amplifying the second, and so without a connecting "and." The "glory to God," which the new-born "Saviour" was to bring, is the first note of this sublime hymn: to this answers, in the second clause, the "peace on earth," of which He was to be "the Prince" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>)--probably sung responsively by the celestial choir; while quickly follows the glad echo of this note, probably by a third detachment of the angelic choristers--"good will to men." "They say not, glory to God in heaven, where angels are, but, using a rare expression, "in the highest [heavens]," whither angels aspire not," (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>) [Bengel]. "Peace" with God is the grand necessity of a fallen world. To bring in this, and all other peace in its train, was the prime errand of the Saviour to this earth, and, along with it, Heaven's whole "good will to men"--the divine complacency on a new footing--descends to rest upon men, as upon the Son Himself, in whom God is "well-pleased." (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>, the same word as here.) <div eID="gen27670" type="x-p"/>
entries.e73dd2fa349f1e138e3ac79b6b3f46898b2513dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14279"/><div sID="gen27671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14279"/><hi type="bold">15. Let us go, &c.--</hi>lovely simplicity of devoutness and faith this! <hi type="bold">They are not taken up with the angels, the glory that invested them, and the lofty strains with which they filled the air. Nor do they say, Let us go and see if this be true--</hi>they have no misgivings. But "Let us go and see this thing which is come to pass, which the Lord hath made known unto us." Does not this confirm the view given on <reference osisRef="Luke.2.8">Lu 2:8</reference> of the spirit of these humble men? <div eID="gen27671" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f66ae87dd1cf2899052a65ac138ff39b27b60bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14280"/><div sID="gen27672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14280"/><hi type="bold">16. with haste--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.39">Lu 1:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.8">Mt 28:8</reference> ("did run"); <reference osisRef="John.4.28">Joh 4:28</reference> ("left her water-pot," as they do their flocks, in a transport).<div eID="gen27672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found Mary, &c.--</hi>"mysteriously guided by the Spirit to the right place through the obscurity of the night" [Olshausen].<div eID="gen27673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a manger--</hi>"the manger," as before. <div eID="gen27674" type="x-p"/>
entries.690ab6dcd8044db701f6755dedd8549d3c4d0800: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14281"/><div sID="gen27675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14281"/><hi type="bold">17. made known abroad--</hi>before their return (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.20">Lu 2:20</reference>), and thus were the first evangelists [Bengel]. <div eID="gen27675" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2fb593747197cb366fbc5e18f4b6bf689ffdca4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14282"/><div sID="gen27676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14282"/><hi type="bold">20. glorifying and praising God, &c.--</hi>The latter word, used of the song of the angels (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.13">Lu 2:13</reference>), and in <reference osisRef="Luke.19.37">Lu 19:37</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Luke.24.53">Lu 24:53</reference>, leads us to suppose that theirs was a song too, probably some canticle from the Psalter--meet vehicle for the swelling emotions of their simple hearts at what "they had heard and seen."<div eID="gen27676" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.2.21">Lu 2:21</reference>. Circumcision of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Here only recorded, and even here merely alluded to, for the sake of the name then given to the holy Babe, "Jesus," or Saviour (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Mt 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.23">Ac 13:23</reference>). Yet in this naming of Him "Saviour," in the act of circumcising Him, which was a symbolical and bloody removal of the body of sin, we have a tacit intimation that they "had need"--</hi>as John said of His Baptism--rather to be circumcised by Him "with the circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the body [of the sins] of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col 2:11</reference>), and that He only "suffered it to be so, because thus it became Him to fulfil all righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.15">Mt 3:15</reference>). Still the circumcision of Christ had a profound bearing on His own work--by few rightly apprehended. For since "he that is circumcised is a debtor to do the whole law" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.3">Ga 5:3</reference>), Jesus thus bore about with Him in His very flesh the seal of a voluntary obligation to do the whole law--by Him only possible in the flesh since the fall. And as He was "made under the law" for no ends of His own, but only "to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Ga 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.5">5</reference>), the obedience to which His circumcision pledged Him was a redeeming obedience--that of a "Saviour." And, finally, as "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law" by "being made a curse for us" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Ga 3:13</reference>), we must regard Him, in His circumcision, as brought under a palpable pledge to be "obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.8">Php 2:8</reference>). <div eID="gen27677" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a69710930762c78d8aa396f82ed2833b7a7fd48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14283"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.2.22-Luke.2.40">Lu 2:22-40</reference>. Purification of the Virgin--Presentation of the Babe in the Temple-Scene There with Simeon and Anna.</title> <div sID="gen27678" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14283"/><hi type="bold">22-24. her purification--</hi>Though the most and best copies read "their," it was the mother only who needed purifying from the legal uncleanness of childbearing. "The days" of this purification for a male child were forty in all (<reference osisRef="Lev.12.2">Le 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.12.4">4</reference>), on the expiry of which the mother was required to offer a lamb for a burnt offering, and a turtle dove or a young pigeon for a sin offering. If she could not afford a lamb, the mother had to bring another turtle dove or young pigeon; and, if even this was beyond her means, then a portion of fine flour, but without the usual fragrant accompaniments of oil and frankincense, as it represented a sin offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.12.6-Lev.8.5">Le 12:6-8; 5</reference>:<reference osisRef="Lev.8.7-Lev.8.11">7-11</reference>). From the intermediate offering of "a pair of turtle doves or two young pigeons," we gather that Joseph and the Virgin were in poor circumstances (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2Co 8:9</reference>), though not in abject poverty. Being a first-born male, they "bring him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord." All such had been claimed as "holy to the Lord," or set apart to sacred uses, in memory of the deliverance of the first-born of Israel from destruction in Egypt, through the sprinkling of blood (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.2">Ex 13:2</reference>). In lieu of these, however, one whole tribe, that of Levi, was accepted, and set apart to occupations exclusively sacred (<reference osisRef="Num.3.11-Num.3.38">Nu 3:11-38</reference>); and whereas there were two hundred seventy-three fewer Levites than first-born of all Israel on the first reckoning, each of these first-born was to be redeemed by the payment of five shekels, yet not without being "presented (or brought) unto the Lord," in token of His rightful claim to them and their service (Nu 3:44-47; 18:<reference osisRef="Num.15.16">15, 16</reference>). It was in obedience to this "law of Moses," that the Virgin presented her babe unto the Lord, "in the east gate of the court called Nicanor's Gate, where she herself would be sprinkled by the priest with the blood of her sacrifice" [Lightfoot]. By that Babe, in due time, we were to be redeemed, "not with corruptible things as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pe 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>), and the consuming of the mother's burnt offering, and the sprinkling of her with the blood of her sin offering, were to find their abiding realization in the "living sacrifice" of the Christian mother herself, in the fulness of a "heart sprinkled from an evil conscience," by "the blood which cleanseth from all sin." <div eID="gen27678" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5c857bf1f479278f496a0d10b3ab9d110c6d254: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14284"/><div sID="gen27679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14284"/><hi type="bold">25. just--</hi>upright in his moral character.<div eID="gen27679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devout--</hi>of a religious frame of spirit.<div eID="gen27680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waiting for the consolation of Israel--</hi>a beautiful title of the coming Messiah, here intended.<div eID="gen27681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Holy Ghost was--</hi>supernaturally.<div eID="gen27682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon him--</hi>Thus was the Spirit, after a dreary absence of nearly four hundred years, returning to the Church, to quicken expectation, and prepare for coming events. <div eID="gen27683" type="x-p"/>
entries.0270ce473ccf843fd56b2ba3bc156fc2b3b13ed2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14285"/><div sID="gen27684" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14285"/><hi type="bold">26. revealed by the Holy Ghost--</hi>implying, beyond all doubt, the personality of the Spirit.<div eID="gen27684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">should see not death till he had seen--</hi>"sweet antithesis!" [Bengel]. How would the one sight gild the gloom of the other! He was, probably, by this time, advanced in years. <div eID="gen27685" type="x-p"/>
entries.eea179c0e00b8ac80a811f4c3bd28073cfa2b57b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14286"/><div sID="gen27686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14286"/>27-28. The Spirit guided him to the temple at the very moment when the Virgin was about to present Him to the Lord. <div eID="gen27686" type="x-p"/>
entries.466a7f6f5d59cd913376f5e57587e40fa2aec198: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14288"/><div sID="gen27688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14288"/><hi type="bold">29. Lord--</hi>"Master," a word rarely used in the New Testament, and selected here with peculiar propriety, when the aged saint, feeling that his last object in wishing to live had now been attained, only awaited his Master's word of command to "depart."<div eID="gen27688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now lettest, &c.--</hi>more clearly, "now Thou art releasing Thy servant"; a patient yet reverential mode of expressing a desire to depart. <div eID="gen27689" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfbbaf5bf9baebbb3b1dc7bd9cfa85aad3b92736: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14289"/><div sID="gen27690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14289"/><hi type="bold">30. seen thy salvation--</hi>Many saw this child, nay, the full-grown "man, Christ Jesus," who never saw in Him "God's Salvation." This estimate of an object of sight, an unconscious, helpless babe, was pure faith. He "beheld His glory" (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>). In another view it was prior faith rewarded by present sight. <div eID="gen27690" type="x-p"/>
entries.9429ddf7cb22c78e58256b780c2073e4f7ff9159: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14290"/><div sID="gen27691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14290"/><hi type="bold">31-32. all people--</hi>all the peoples, mankind at large.<div eID="gen27691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a light to the Gentiles--</hi>then in thick darkness.<div eID="gen27692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory of thy people Israel--</hi>already Thine, and now, in the believing portion of it, to be so more gloriously than ever. It will be observed that this "swan-like song, bidding an eternal farewell to this terrestrial life" [Olshausen], takes a more comprehensive view of the kingdom of Christ than that of Zacharias, though the kingdom they sing of is one. <div eID="gen27693" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a1fc3c9039f3bbc06d554f1186d2d6d3377228d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14291"/><div sID="gen27694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14291"/><hi type="bold">34-35. set--</hi>appointed.<div eID="gen27694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign spoken against--</hi>Perhaps the former of these phrases expresses the two stages of temporary "fall of many in Israel" through unbelief, during our Lord's earthly career, and the subsequent "rising again" of the same persons after the effusion of the Spirit at pentecost threw a new light to them on the whole subject; while the latter clause describes the determined enemies of the Lord Jesus. Such opposite views of Christ are taken from age to age. <div eID="gen27695" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4c06cb6775570a80d0c6faebaca2f34c084378b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14293"/><div sID="gen27698" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14293"/><hi type="bold">36. Anna--</hi>or, Hannah.<div eID="gen27698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a prophetess--</hi>another evidence that "the last times" in which God was to "pour out His Spirit upon all flesh" were at hand.<div eID="gen27699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the tribe of Aser--</hi>one of the ten tribes, of whom many were not carried captive, and not a few reunited themselves to Judah after the return from Babylon. The distinction of tribes, though practically destroyed by the captivity, was well enough known up to their final dispersion (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Ro 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.14">He 7:14</reference>); nor is it now entirely lost.<div eID="gen27700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lived, &c.--</hi>she had lived seven years with her husband (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.36">Lu 2:36</reference>), and been a widow eighty-four years; so that if she married at the earliest marriageable age, twelve years, she could not at this time be less than a hundred three years old. <div eID="gen27701" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b92c0e223b7f5e339f33909d6953e96c8dae72e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14294"/><div sID="gen27702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14294"/><hi type="bold">37. departed not from the temple--</hi>was found there at all stated hours of the day, and even during the night services of the temple watchmen (<reference osisRef="Ps.134.1">Psa 134:1</reference>, 2), "serving God with fastings and prayer." (See <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.5">1Ti 5:5</reference>, suggested by this.) <div eID="gen27702" type="x-p"/>
entries.c24c694559c1d09a34575ca783795c1e253baa9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14295"/><div sID="gen27703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14295"/><hi type="bold">38. coming in--</hi>"presenting herself." She had been there already but now is found "standing by," as Simeon's testimony to the blessed Babe died away, ready to take it up "in turn" (as the word rendered "likewise" here means).<div eID="gen27703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to all them, &c.--</hi>the sense is, "to all them in Jerusalem that were looking for redemption"--saying in effect, In that Babe are wrapt up all your expectations. If this was at the hour of prayer, when numbers flocked to the temple, it would account for her having such an audience as the words imply [Alford]. <div eID="gen27704" type="x-p"/>
entries.764fbe94704da2cf0157d8e4e8a8e2c9b8535577: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14296"/><div sID="gen27705" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14296"/>39. Nothing is more difficult than to fix the precise order in which the visit of the Magi, with the flight into and return from Egypt (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.13-Matt.2.23">Mt 2:13-23</reference>), are to be taken, in relation to the circumcision and presentation of Christ in the temple, here recorded. It is perhaps best to leave this in the obscurity in which we find it, as the result of two independent, though if we knew all, easily reconcilable narratives. <div eID="gen27705" type="x-p"/>
entries.61635c7143389a428d4e1a74da028658bc878712: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14297"/><div sID="gen27706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14297"/>40. His mental development kept pace with His bodily, and "the grace of God," the divine favor, rested manifestly and increasingly upon Him. See <reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">Lu 2:52</reference>.<div eID="gen27706" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.2.41-Luke.2.52">Lu 2:41-52</reference>. First Conscious Visit to Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen27707" type="x-p"/> "Solitary flowered out of the wonderful enclosed garden of the thirty years, plucked precisely there where the swollen bud, at a distinctive crisis (at twelve years of age), bursts into flower. To mark that is assuredly the design and the meaning of this record" [Stier]. <div eID="gen27707" type="x-p"/>
entries.21d7a909b42492c17b6fecf52d4bec298d00542d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14298"/><div sID="gen27708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14298"/><hi type="bold">42. went up--</hi>"were wont to go." Though males only were required to go up to Jerusalem at the three annual festivals (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.14-Exod.23.17">Ex 23:14-17</reference>), devout women, when family duties permitted, went also, as did Hannah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.7">1Sa 1:7</reference>), and, as we here see, the mother of Jesus.<div eID="gen27708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when twelve years old--</hi>At this age every Jewish boy was styled "a son of the law," being put under a course of instruction and trained to fasting and attendance on public worship, besides being set to learn a trade. At this age accordingly our Lord is taken up for the first time to Jerusalem, at the passover season, the chief of the three annual festivals. But oh, with what thoughts and feelings must this Youth have gone up! Long ere He beheld it, He had doubtless "loved the habitation of God's house and the place where His honor dwelt" (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.8">Psa 26:8</reference>), a love nourished, we may be sure, by that "word hid in His heart," with which in afterlife He showed so perfect a familiarity. As the time for His first visit approached, could one's ear have caught the breathings of His young soul, he might have heard Him whispering, "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after Thee, O God. The Lord loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go unto the house of the Lord. Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem!" (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.1">Psa 42:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.87.2">87:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.122.1">122:1</reference>, 2). On catching the first view of "the city of their solemnities," and high above all in it, "the place of God's rest," we hear Him saying to Himself, "Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth is Mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King: Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God doth shine" (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">50:2</reference>). Of His feelings or actions during all the eight days of the feast not a word is said. As a devout child, in company with its parents, He would go through the services, keeping His thoughts to Himself. But methinks I hear Him, after the sublime services of that feast, saying to Himself, "He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.3">So 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen27709" type="x-p"/>
entries.287491444d99a7805987e351abe517fa74c249b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14299"/><div sID="gen27710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14299"/><hi type="bold">43. as they returned--</hi>If the duties of life must give place to worship, worship, in its turn, must give place to them. Jerusalem is good, but Nazareth is good, too; let him who neglects the one, on pretext of attending to the other, ponder this scene.<div eID="gen27710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tarried behind ... Joseph and his mother knew not--</hi>Accustomed to the discretion and obedience of the lad [Olshausen], they might be thrown off their guard. <div eID="gen27711" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d57bf83fe320a1ccf0fb92a7f26c3be2aa69c73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14300"/><div sID="gen27712" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14300"/><hi type="bold">44. sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintances--</hi>On these sacred journeys, whole villages and districts travelled in groups together, partly for protection, partly for company; and as the well-disposed would beguile the tediousness of the way by good discourse, to which the child Jesus would be no silent listener, they expect to find Him in such a group. <div eID="gen27712" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fb36039d444a3fece4937f471f3b16e6db2df30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14301"/><div sID="gen27713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14301"/><hi type="bold">45-46. After three sorrowing days, they find Him still in Jerusalem, not gazing on its architecture, or surveying its forms of busy life, but in the temple--</hi>not the "sanctuary" (as in <reference osisRef="Luke.1.9">Lu 1:9</reference>), to which only the priests had access, but in some one of the enclosures around it, where the rabbins, or "doctors," taught their scholars. <div eID="gen27713" type="x-p"/>
entries.6005a9e140179b0946e3eac4afc4d1eeeffe38a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14303"/><div sID="gen27715" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14303"/><hi type="bold">49. about my Father's business--</hi>literally, "in" or "at My Fathers," that is, either "about My Father's affairs," or "in My Father's courts"--where He dwells and is to be found--about His hand, so to speak. This latter shade of meaning, which includes the former, is perhaps the true one, Here He felt Himself at home, breathing His own proper air. His words convey a gentle rebuke of their obtuseness in requiring Him to explain this. "Once here, thought ye I should so readily hasten away? Let ordinary worshippers be content to keep the feast and be gone; but is this all ye have learnt of Me?" Methinks we are here let into the holy privacies of Nazareth; for what He says they should have known, He must have given them ground to know. She tells Him of the sorrow with which His father and she had sought Him. He speaks of no Father but one, saying, in effect, My Father has not been seeking Me; I have been with Him all this time; "the King hath brought me into His chambers ... His left hand is under my head, and His right hand doth embrace me" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference>; 2:6). How is it that ye do not understand? (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.21">Mr 8:21</reference>). <div eID="gen27715" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1858090eab5ee8440262ec8cfdae68330ee4cdc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14304"/><div sID="gen27716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14304"/><hi type="bold">50-51. understood not--</hi>probably He had never expressly said as much, and so confounded them, though it was but the true interpretation of many things which they had seen and heard from Him at home. (See on <reference osisRef="John.14.4">Joh 14:4</reference>.) But lest it should be thought that now He threw off the filial yoke, and became His own Master henceforth, and theirs too, it is purposely added, "And He went down with them, and was subject unto them." The marvel of this condescension lies in its coming after such a scene, and such an assertion of His higher Sonship; and the words are evidently meant to convey this. "From this time we have no more mention of Joseph. The next we hear is of his "mother and brethren" (<reference osisRef="John.2.12">Joh 2:12</reference>); whence it is inferred, that between this time and the commencement of our Lord's public life, Joseph died" [Alford], having now served the double end of being the protector of our Lord's Virgin--mother, and affording Himself the opportunity of presenting a matchless pattern of subjection to both parents. <div eID="gen27716" type="x-p"/>
entries.88c799f3efe79fae5aaee6b7ba90b003f3c2b4ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14305"/><div sID="gen27717" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14305"/>52. See on <reference osisRef="Luke.2.40">Lu 2:40</reference>.<div eID="gen27717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stature--</hi>or better, perhaps, as in the Margin, "age," which implies the other. This is all the record we have of the next eighteen years of that wondrous life. What seasons of tranquil meditation over the lively oracles, and holy fellowship with His Father; what inlettings, on the one hand, of light, and love, and power from on high, and outgoings of filial supplication, freedom, love, and joy on the other, would these eighteen years contain! And would they not seem "but a few days" if they were so passed, however ardently He might long to be more directly "about His Father's business?" <chapter eID="Luke.2"/>

entries.e47ba8e6974f8ac107c33c895baed978a568467d: <div eID="gen39911" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39912" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39913" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39913" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39912" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39914" type="x-p"/> The decree of Augustus to enroll all the Roman empire, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.1">Luk 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.2">Luk 2:2</reference>. Joseph and Mary go to their own city to be enrolled, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.3-Luk.2.5">Luk 2:3-5</reference>. Christ is born, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.6">Luk 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.7">Luk 2:7</reference>. His birth is announced to the shepherds, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.8-Luk.2.14">Luk 2:8-14</reference>. They go to Bethlehem, and find Joseph, Mary, and Christ, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.15-Luk.2.20">Luk 2:15-20</reference>. Christ is circumcised, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.21">Luk 2:21</reference>. His parents go to present him in the temple, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.22-Luk.2.24">Luk 2:22-24</reference>. Simeon receives him: his song, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.25-Luk.2.35">Luk 2:25-35</reference>. Anna the prophetess, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.36-Luk.2.38">Luk 2:36-38</reference>. The holy family return to Nazareth, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.39">Luk 2:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.40">Luk 2:40</reference>. They go to Jerusalem at the feast of the passover, and leave Jesus behind in Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.41-Luk.2.44">Luk 2:41-44</reference>. They return seeking him, and find him in the midst of the doctors, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.45-Luk.2.47">Luk 2:45-47</reference>. His mother chides him, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.48">Luk 2:48</reference>. His defense of his conduct, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.49">Luk 2:49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.50">Luk 2:50</reference>. They all return to Nazareth, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.51">Luk 2:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.52">Luk 2:52</reference>. <div eID="gen39914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39915" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39916" type="x-p"/> Caesar Augustus - This was Caius Caesar Octavianus Augustus, who was proclaimed emperor of Rome in the 29th year before our Lord, and died a.d. 14. <div eID="gen39916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39917" type="x-p"/> That all the world should be taxed - Πασαν την οικουμενην, the whole of that empire. It is agreed, on all hands, that this cannot mean the whole world, as in the common translation; for this very sufficient reason, that the Romans had not the dominion of the whole earth, and therefore could have no right to raise levies or taxes in those places to which their dominion did not extend. Οικουμενη signifies properly the inhabited part of the earth, from οικεω, to dwell, or inhabit. Polybius makes use of the very words in this text to point out the extent of the Roman government, lib. vi. c. 48; and Plutarch uses the word in exactly the same sense, Pomp. p. 635. See the passages in Wetstein. Therefore the whole that could be meant here, can be no more than that a general Census of the inhabitants and their effects had been made in the reign of Augustus, through all the Roman dominions. <div eID="gen39917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39918" type="x-p"/> But as there is no general census mentioned in any historian as having taken place at this time, the meaning of οικουμενη must be farther restrained, and applied solely to the land of Judea. This signification it certainly has in this same evangelist, <reference osisRef="Luk.21.26">Luk 21:26</reference>. Men's hearts failing them for fear, and for looking after those things which are coming on the earth, τῃ οικουμενῃ this land. The whole discourse relates to the calamities that were coming, not upon the whole world, nor the whole of the Roman empire, but on the land of Judea, see <reference osisRef="Luk.21.21">Luk 21:21</reference>. Then let them that are in Judea flee to the mountains. Out of Judea, therefore, there would be safety; and only those who should be with child, or giving suck, in those days, are considered as peculiarly unhappy, because they could not flee away from that land on which the scourge was to fall: for the wrath, or punishment, shall be, says our Lord, εν τῳ λαῳ τουτῳ, On This Very People, viz. the Jews, <reference osisRef="Luk.21.23">Luk 21:23</reference>. It appears that St. Luke used this word in this sense in conformity to the Septuagint, who have applied it in precisely the same way, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Isa 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.26">Isa 14:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">Isa 24:1</reference>. And from this we may learn, that the word οικουμενη had been long used as a term by which the land of Judea was commonly expressed. Ἡ γη, which signifies the earth, or world in general, is frequently restrained to this sense, being often used by the evangelists and others for all the country of Judea. See <reference osisRef="Luk.4.25">Luk 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jos.2.3">Jos 2:3</reference>. <div eID="gen39918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39919" type="x-p"/> It is probable that the reason why this enrolment, or census, is said to have been throughout the whole Jewish nation, was to distinguish it from that partial one, made ten years after, mentioned <reference osisRef="Act.5.37">Act 5:37</reference>, which does not appear to have extended beyond the estates of Archelaus, and which gave birth to the insurrection excited by Judas of Galilee. See Josephus, Ant. book xx. c. 3.
entries.d8916612240090adba0f77543080f42e70802987: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39920" type="x-p"/> This taxing was first made when Cyrenius, etc. - The next difficulty in this text is found in this verse, which may be translated, Now this first enrolment was made when Quirinus was governor of Syria. <div eID="gen39920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39921" type="x-p"/> It is easily proved, and has been proved often, that Caius Sulpicius Quirinus, the person mentioned in the text, was not governor of Syria, till ten or twelve years after the birth of our Lord. <div eID="gen39921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39922" type="x-p"/> St. Matthew says that our Lord was born in the reign of Herod, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.1">Luk 2:1</reference>, at which time Quintilius Varus was president of Syria, (Joseph. Ant. book xvii. c. 5, sect. 2), who was preceded in that office by Sentius Saturninus. Cyrenius, or Quirinus, was not sent into Syria till Archelaus was removed from the government of Judea; and Archelaus had reigned there between nine and ten years after the death of Herod; so that it is impossible that the census mentioned by the evangelist could have been made in the presidency of Quirinus. <div eID="gen39922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39923" type="x-p"/> Several learned men have produced solutions of this difficulty; and, indeed, there are various ways of solving it, which may be seen at length in Lardner, vol. i. p. 248-329. One or other of the two following appears to me to be the true meaning of the text. <div eID="gen39923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39924" type="x-p"/> 1. When Augustus published this decree, it is supposed that Quirinus, who was a very active man, and a person in whom the emperor confided, was sent into Syria and Judea with extraordinary powers, to make the census here mentioned; though, at that time, he was not governor of Syria, for Quintilius Varus was then president; and that when he came, ten or twelve years after, into the presidency of Syria, there was another census made, to both of which St. Luke alludes, when he says, This was the first assessment of Cyrenius, governor of Syria; for so Dr. Lardner translates the words. The passage, thus translated, does not say that this assessment was made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria, which would not have been the truth, but that this was the first assessment which Cyrenius, who was (i.e. afterwards) governor of Syria, made; for after he became governor, he made a second. Lardner defends this opinion in a very satisfactory and masterly manner. See vol. i. p. 317. etc. <div eID="gen39924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39925" type="x-p"/> 2. The second way of solving this difficulty is by translating the words thus: This enrolment was made Before Cyrenius was governor of Syria; or, before that of Cyrenius. This sense the word πρωτος appears to have, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.30">Joh 1:30</reference> : ὁτι πρωτος μου ην, for he was Before me. <reference osisRef="Joh.15.18">Joh 15:18</reference> : The world hated me Before (πρωτον) it hated you. See also <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.43">2Sam 19:43</reference>. Instead of πρωτη, some critics read προ της, This enrolment was made Before That of Cyrenius. Michaelis; and some other eminent and learned men, have been of this opinion: but their conjecture is not supported by any MS. yet discovered; nor, indeed, is there any occasion for it. As the words in the evangelist are very ambiguous, the second solution appears to me to be the best.
entries.3babd0a6411afce5a30b86898306f793534c4928: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39926" type="x-p"/> And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city - The Roman census was an institution of Servius Tullius, sixth king of Rome. From the account which Dionysius of Halicarnassus gives of it; we may at once see its nature. "He ordered all the citizens of Rome to register their estates according to their value in money, taking an oath, in a form he prescribed, to deliver a faithful account according to the best of their knowledge, specifying the names of their parents, their own age, the names of their wives and children, adding also what quarter of the city, or what town in the country, they lived in." Ant. Rom. l. iv. c. 15. p. 212. Edit. Huds. <div eID="gen39926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39927" type="x-p"/> A Roman census appears to have consisted of these two parts: <div eID="gen39927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39928" type="x-p"/> 1. The account which the people were obliged to give in of their names, quality, employments, wives, children, servants, and estates; and <div eID="gen39928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39929" type="x-p"/> 2. The value set upon the estates by the censors, and the proportion in which they adjudged them to contribute to the defense and support of the state, either in men or money, or both: and this seems to have been the design of the census or enrolment in the text. <div eID="gen39929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39930" type="x-p"/> This census was probably similar to that made in England in the reign of William the Conqueror, which is contained in what is termed Domesday Book, now in the Chapter House, Westminster, and dated 1086.
entries.240f99da28737045464f5b2f88df46b4e84adb05: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen39930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39931" type="x-p"/> With Mary his espoused wife - There was no necessity for Mary to have gone to Bethlehem, as Joseph's presence could have answered the end proposed in the census as well without Mary as with her; but God so ordered it, that the prophecy of Micah should be thus fulfilled, and that Jesus should be born in the city of David; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mic 5:2</reference>.
entries.3321acb08cb36b8edb636c6314322ef1901cb2a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen39931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39932" type="x-p"/> Laid him in a manger - Wetstein has shown, from a multitude of instances, that φατνη means not merely the manger, but the whole stable, and this I think is its proper meaning in this place. The Latins use praesepe, a manger, in the same sense. So Virgil, Aen. vii. p. 275. <div eID="gen39932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39933" type="x-p"/> Stabant ter centum nitidi in praesepibus altis "Three hundred sleek horses stood in lofty stables." <div eID="gen39933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39934" type="x-p"/> Many have thought that this was a full proof of the meanness and poverty of the holy family, that they were obliged to take up their lodging in a stable; but such people overlook the reason given by the inspired penman, because there was no room for them in the inn. As multitudes were going now to be enrolled, all the lodgings in the inn had been occupied before Joseph and Mary arrived. An honest man who had worked diligently at his business, under the peculiar blessing of God, as Joseph undoubtedly had, could not have been so destitute of money as not to be able to procure himself and wife a comfortable lodging for a night; and, had he been so ill fitted for the journey as some unwarrantably imagine, we may take it for granted he would not have brought his wife with him, who was in such a state as not to be exposed to any inconveniences of this kind without imminent danger. <div eID="gen39934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39935" type="x-p"/> There was no room for them in the inn - In ancient times, inns were as respectable as they were useful, being fitted up for the reception of travelers alone: - now, they are frequently haunts for the idle and the profligate, the drunkard and the infidel; - in short, for any kind of guests except Jesus and his genuine followers. To this day there is little room for such in most inns; nor indeed have they, in general, any business in such places. As the Hindoos travel in large companies to holy places and to festivals, it often happens that the inns (suraies) are so crowded that there is not room for one half of them: some lie at the door, others in the porch. These inns, or lodging-houses, are kept by Mohammedans, and Mussulmans obtain prepared food at them; but the Hindoos purchase rice, etc., and cook it, paying about a halfpenny a night for their lodging. Ward's Customs.
entries.7ac1cf0914134ad5157f51887e6e0187324c1bdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen39935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39936" type="x-p"/> There were - shepherds abiding in the field - There is no intimation here that these shepherds were exposed to the open air. They dwelt in the fields where they had their sheep penned up; but they undoubtedly had tents or booths under which they dwelt. <div eID="gen39936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39937" type="x-p"/> Keeping watch - by night - Or, as in the margin, keeping the watches of the night, i.e. each one keeping a watch (which ordinarily consisted of three hours) in his turn. The reason why they watched them in the field appears to have been, either to preserve the sheep from beasts of prey, such as wolves, foxes, etc., or from freebooting banditti, with which all the land of Judea was at that time much infested. It was a custom among the Jews to send out their sheep to the deserts, about the passover, and bring them home at the commencement of the first rain: during the time they were out, the shepherds watched them night and day. As the passover occurred in the spring, and the first rain began early in the month of Marchesvan, which answers to part of our October and November, we find that the sheep were kept out in the open country during the whole of the summer. And as these shepherds had not yet brought home their flocks, it is a presumptive argument that October had not yet commenced, and that, consequently, our Lord was not born on the 25th of December, when no flocks were out in the fields; nor could he have been born later than September, as the flocks were still in the fields by night.
